utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, I see Mr. Piletta-Zanin is not there. He will have a delay in travelling, do you expect, or...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, due to his commitments in Geneva, my colleague is not going to be present today. However, as of tomorrow, he will be here with me again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think before we continue with the witnesses, we still have to deal with the admission into evidence of the documents tendered during the testimony of Mr. Kundo and Witness AE. Madam Registrar, could you please guide me through the documents. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. Before that happens, on Friday morning, Mr. Piletta-Zanin made some submissions in relation to the medical documentation in respect of Mr. Kundo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am ready to respond to that. If you wish it, Mr. President, if you think it is necessary, I would give a brief explanation as to why the documents -- why there were two or more versions of the medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translations. Of the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. The differences in the translation are clearly on the face of the documents explained by different or varying qualities of legibility. So the issue then becomes why is there more than one version of the document? And the explanation for that I think is apparent when one looks more carefully at the ERN numbers and reflects on the evidence that was given on Friday. If you wish, I could briefly give that explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would do it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the exhibit list, the Prosecution has placed two versions of the medical report. They are Exhibit Numbers P1800 and P1809. During the evidence of Mrs. Kundo, she was taken to -- by the Defence, she was taken to an investigative report done by the Bosnian authorities at the time. You may recall that she was asked questions about a statement given by her husband.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will slow down in deference to the interpreters. I apologise. That report, of course, had been disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence. The ERN numbers for that report range from 0028-4041 through to 49. In other words, when the report was received by the Tribunal, it was stamped with those numbers. The report included the letter of discharge, and therefore, not surprisingly, that's where it picked up the first ERN number, which ends in 47. And that, in turn, when one looks at the two translations attached, the translation attached to each of the exhibits, one sees down at the bottom of one of those translations that the document is based on a medical report within that same range, that is, 47. One then goes to, in time, the statement taken by the investigator, an investigator of the OTP, of Mrs. Kundo. And you may recall that during the testimony of Mrs. Kundo, I took her to a part of one of her statements which referred to a medical report which was stated to be attached to her statement. One sees in the statement, having regard to the ERN numbers, that at that point, the medical document picks up its second ERN number. We then see -- so that explains one of the exhibits on the exhibit list in relation to the medical report, Exhibit 18 -- one of the versions on Exhibit 1800. There then came into the possession of the OTP a copy of the document from a different source, and inquiries reveal that that source was a Dr. Kulenovic, who was the head of the relevant clinical centre. But in relation to the other exhibit, one sees that on the face of the document, there are a number of additional signatures. That is explained by the fact that 1809, in particular, the first version of that report, is attached to the 92 bis statement authenticated by Kapetanovic, first name Faris, in relation to hospital records from Kosevo Hospital. So when one looks closely at the various stamps and signatures on the face of that document, it becomes readily apparent that one of those signatures is in relation to that person completing their 92 bis statement. And there should be, behind it, an earlier version of the same record which lacks that 92 bis attestation. So Mr. President, that's the explanation for the various copies of the document. The reason that we have tendered two of them is that one is more legible than the other in various parts. And that is, of course, why each of the two translations has differences. Again, the basic proposition is simply whether there is evidence of the injury, the wounding, consistent with the history of the wounding. That comes primarily from the witness. One then goes to the documentation, if there is any available, for corroboration. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you one question: Of course, the Chamber noticed the double ERN numbers, what the explanation is, that's not difficult to understand. The Defence has also pointed at some inconsistencies in the translations, and not just legibility. And I think there are also sometimes it seems that the translation of stamps is not always clearly distinguished from the translation of text. So what about the inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, many of the parts of the translations marked by Mr. Piletta-Zanin in ink are, in fact, explained by the lack of legibility. To give an example, under the box dated "Admission" in the copy marked in blue, we simply see "2 November." When one looks at the original of that translation, one can see "2.11." and the year is not apparent. When one looks at the original for the other translation, and that translation shows "2 November 1993," one can clearly see the original -- the date, rather, on the face of the document. I note in relation to that that there appears to be a handwritten entry under date of admission. That is, on P1809. It therefore appears that someone at a later point has written in the date. I note the date is the same as on the earlier version, and one can only speculate that perhaps the date on the copy of the document retained by the hospital was not legible or fully legible, so it has been corrected. But there is no inconsistency. As to any inconsistencies on the face of the translations, that is really a matter for the translation unit. In other words, the OTP puts in a request for the translation and whatever we receive, we then attach to the document that we tender. Mr. President, I do not note any significant difference between the translations. One of the issues that I recall that Mr. Piletta-Zanin drew our attention to was the signature of the doctor as translated and marked by him in pink. And essentially, he defied anyone to read from the original that name. Mr. President, I do note that at the bottom of that same original, one sees the stamp of the same name. One can barely make out the surname in the box "Head of clinic signed" halfway down the form on the right-hand side. I can certainly make out the last four letters, and the first capital letter, first capital letter being "K," last four letters being "O-V-I-C." When one looks at the Stamp at the bottom of the page towards the middle, one sees that it is a stamp for Dr. Faruk Kulenovic. And it may well be - it's a matter of speculation - that the translator assumed that was the same person and took the information from that stamp. The issue is really whether there is, firstly, any challenge by the Defence on the material in the medical report; and if so, whether the authenticity becomes an issue. The witness has given evidence of the document, so there is evidence before the Tribunal already, before we get to the 92 bis statement, to the effect that the original, that is, the photocopies from which the translations were done, are in fact the relevant medical report. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, the Defence has pointed to the problem of illegibility of the medical documentation several times. The problem was often raised at the meetings with my colleagues from the Prosecution. The same problem arose this time, and it involved the problems of translation of certain documents. The Defence declared its objection to the authenticity of the entire medical documentation. We were -- we have been able to see the document in respect of Ms. Kundo, which was illegible, and we believe that it is possible that there are several such documents in the Serbian language, and that that was the reason for differences in translation. Because of the contents of each medical document where it is stated that the patient was hit by a sniper bullet, which information was not entered as part of the case history but the conclusion of the physician, we object to the document itself, because such a conclusion can only be made by a pathologist, by a forensic expert. We have pointed out the problems of the documents, and the reason for our objection is impossibility for the Defence to study these documents. We have requested access to original documents several times. I think that Ramiza Kundo told us that she had the original of this document. If such a document exists in its original form, I don't see any reason why should we continue to waste any more time in order to establish the authenticity of the documents which are obviously illegible. We maintain our request for access to the originals because we believe that it would be possible for us, by doing so, to assess the veracity of the documents which are provided to the Defence and the Chamber. And of course, it will be up to the Chamber to judge the value of the documents. Therefore, it is our conclusion and our motion that the original documents should be made accessible so that we can establish its authenticity. And I believe we have stated often times the reason why we challenge the authenticity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give a decision on the specific matter after the break. That just concerns, I would, say the medical documentation of Ramiza Kundo. Madam Registrar, what other documents do we have to decide upon?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the list I have, it's Prosecution Exhibit P3280V, P3279V, P1800, P1800.1, P1811, P1811A, P3673 and P3674. That's what I have. Apart from the documents that were discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you're repeating, I think, part of the documents, because we discussed 1800. Well, let's just start at the beginning. The video and the second number you mentioned, that was the 360-degree photograph, they are admitted. Then 1800 and translations, we'll give a decision on that after the break. Then you said 1811, that was -- could you perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: A colour copy of a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Coloured copy of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And P1811A is the black and white copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was the double-sided copy, as far as I remember. The major importance was that the photocopy, the testimony was that it was signed but the signature was not visible on the photocopy. So 1811, a coloured photograph with markings on it, is admitted into evidence. And also 1811.A, which is the same photograph in black and white, and at the back of the photograph, some handwritten information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, 1811 is the coloured version. Thank you. And 1811A is the black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I intended to say, at least. Then we have 36 -- I first had 72 as a name sheet of Witness AE, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought we would deal with these witnesses separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first Mrs. Kundo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 3673, could you please assist me. That is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the witness statement, but -- yes, the witness statement is admitted in evidence, but since the attachment to the statement is not translated and this translation concerns similar aspects as the translation of Document 1800, the attachment is not yet admitted. We'll decide upon that after the break as well. And then we have 3674. You said that's the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's another witness statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Another witness statement of the month of October, 30 October, 3674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's admitted as well. Then we come to the next witness, that was Witness AE.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The following exhibits are P3363, medical record; and P3672, that's an under seal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3672 is a name sheet. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that 3365 is the medical record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look and check it. It's 3365, yes, that's what I have here as well. The name sheet is not a problem. That's 3672. That's admitted under seal. The medical record is also admitted under the specific circumstances of this document itself. The translation covers all parts the Prosecution relies upon. The small part of the document not translated seems to reflect the treatment and the medication of the patient, and the Defence has been confronted with this and has not given any specific reasons why it was material to the Defence that this part also would be translated, apart from the fact that the Defence has knowledge of the B/C/S language and could read it by itself, it nevertheless insisted upon translation of the document as a matter of principle, and that objection is denied. It also has to be admitted under seal, Madam Registrar, because it contains the name of the protected witness. I think, having dealt with the documents, we could now continue. Mr. Ierace, we received a new order of witnesses. Would you please call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness will be taken by Chester Stamp. Might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, am I well informed that Mr. Hamill will be the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, am I well informed that the witness did not arrive yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness was here last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He came from early last week, and he indicated that he would like to go and return. He's from Ireland, and I think he wanted to go somewhere, which did not present an inconvenience. And my last knowledge of the matter that I instructed that he had to be here for this morning, which meant that he would have to return here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or at least this morning, early. Have you any information, any additional information --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just learning now that he's not here. I was assured that he would be here for this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you permit me, Your Honour, I can contact the Victims and Witnesses Section and see how long it will take before the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, if they are aware of where the witness is, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What I heard from the usher, they are aware, and he must be here within 10 minutes. That's the latest information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what would you suggest? If it's just a matter of 10 minutes, it might be more convenient for you to -- not to start with another witness. But if you could change your order, I don't know whether this would...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not quite sure if I could change the order. I don't know if the other witnesses would be here for this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That witness we had expected to take at least today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Well, I think the only thing we could do is to have a short break and urge you to inform the Chamber as soon as possible when there's any information about when we could expect the witness. And I'd like to hear from whoever is responsible for the presence of the witnesses why this could happen. Because one thing was for sure from last Friday, it was clear that we would start this morning with Mr. Hamill. Yes. We'll have a break. Could perhaps, since it has been indicated that it might be take no more than 10 minutes, could everyone stay nearby so that we could immediately resume when the witness is there. Thank you. --- Break taken at 10.04 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, I have been made to understand that there was a misunderstanding between the OTP and the Victims and Witnesses Unit. The victim was here in the building, however at some stage a member of the OTP had indicated to him that perhaps the order had changed. Not -- that perhaps the order had changed. I am told by the Victims and Witnesses Unit that they had been led to believe that the order had changed. That is the explanation for the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's all try to prevent misunderstandings for the future. Mr. Hamill, I don't think I have to ask you whether you hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You speak English. Before giving your testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of the declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hamill. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, then by counsel for the Defence, and if there are any questions by the Judges, you'll hear them. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and rank.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: My name is John Gerard Brendan Hamill. I am a commandant, which is the equivalent of a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which army is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The Irish Army, the Irish Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you been a member of the Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have been 30 years in the Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you worked in any particular field in the Irish Defence Forces in those 30 years?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am an artillery officer and have been since September 1974. I have served overseas with United Nations forces on six occasions, and I have served with the European Community Monitoring Mission also for a period in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in between May 1993 and July 1994, can you tell us where you served, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: At that time, I was a military observer with United Nations in the United Nations Protection Force. I spent three months in the vicinity of Sarajevo, followed by one month in Daruvar, followed by ten months in Zagreb, where I was the deputy chief operations officer for the first four months, and then acting chief operations officer of the UNMO organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where exactly is Daruvar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Daruvar is in sector west in -- the former sector west in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what period of time did you spend as a member of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo or in the vicinity of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was posted there in May 1993, and my posting terminated in August 1993. So apart from two leave periods, I spent from May until the beginning of August in Sarajevo and its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your first posting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, I was posted first to the Lima 5 team, and the following day, to the Lima 8 team. "Lima" indicated Lukavica, that is, the military observers which were operating on the Serb side of the front line. So I was there from day 2 as the team leader of Lima 8, based in Gornji Kotorac. Following a period there, I was taken into the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. headquarters of the UNMO organisation in Lukavica, and I lived in Lukavica barracks for most of the remainder of my period in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is Gornji Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Gornji Kotorac is just to the south of Lukavica. It's a hill or its on a hill called Ilinaca, which is overlooking the airport. It also looks over Vojkovici, Hrasnica, Igman, as far as Stup and Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were an UNMO at Gornji Kotorac, what was the nature of your task?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The nature of the task was to, in that particular area, to visit the Serb weapon positions within my area, and to ensure that they were not being fired. And if they were being fired, to elicit information as to why they were being fired, to attempt to negotiate cease-fires where necessary, and to report on all that I found to my higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Gornji Kotorac is to the south of the city you said, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is. It's to the southeast of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you ever posted in any of the northern parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was posted to the northern part of the city from around mid-July. I was posted first of all to Vogosca, where we had the headquarters of the UNMOs to the north of the city. And from there, I covered from Radava as far as Igman as the commander of the UNMOs in that area. However, due to a problem we had, we moved to Blazuj, which is just beyond Ilidza, on the road towards Mostar and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in those postings towards the north of the city and the south of the city, you indicated that part of your task was to make observations. Did the UNMOs at the time you were there have sufficient personnel and material to make comprehensive observations of all the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my opinion that they did not have sufficient resources available. Large parts of the area were extremely difficult to get at, particularly in the north and east of the city. The furthest east we had in the south was the Lima 5 position in Kasindol. Then you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is to what part of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It's east. Southeast. It's east of Lukavica. So from there, as far as Sombolovac there was no team in situ, and the area was very inaccessible. Also, it was inaccessible as the Bosnian Serb army did not wish us to travel throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the area towards the north of the city? Was that accessible or inaccessible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was partly accessible, partly inaccessible. The terrain was difficult particularly to the northeast, in the area of Radava, and from there eastwards. In the west, the travelling was good, however there were artificial obstacles put in our way on many occasions. There was a group of so-called Chetniks led by a man called Vasilije Vidovic, known as Vasko, who regularly impeded the UNMO teams in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the northeast area, what was your ability to observe?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Similarly in the northeast, it was difficult, again because of the fact that the access to the area was controlled by the same so-called Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were posted in those areas, did you make any observations of the Bosnian Serb army artillery and mortar positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly, if you could in a sentence or two, tell us how mortars and artillery are sited or positioned in the standard military use.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In the standard military use, each type of weapon has its own job. Thus, for example, guns would be used for long-range firing at distant targets, very distant targets. They would be sited, depending on the tactical circumstances, either well to the forward or well to the rear. To the rear, in Defence; and forward, in attack. Mortars would be a lot closer to the front line due to the shorter range. Again, Howitzers and mortars can fire from behind high cover, so they would be used in circumstances of difficult terrain. And the job of the artillery is always to support the combat troops, that is, the infantry. That is, in conventional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In conventional circumstances, in respect to mortars, are they normally sited in one position for a long time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, no. Mortars, because of their high visibility, the slow rate of fire, the ease of detection, are normally used in what we would describe as "shoot and scoot."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is, that they fire a number of rounds very quickly and move to another position, perhaps hundreds of metres, perhaps kilometres distant. That is to prevent what we call "counter battery fire," which is fire directed by artillery at artillery. Again, this is in conventional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you make any particular observation in respect to how mortar positions were sited by the BSA army around Sarajevo while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I was very surprised at the positioning of both mortars and guns. They were not used in the conventional way that I have just described. What they did was they sited any weapon they had, whether mortar or gun, in a particular area and left it there. For example, in the Lima 8 position where I had responsibility for monitoring two troops of mortars --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is Lima 8 position, before you go on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry, Gornji Kotorac. There were two troops of mortars, there was a troop of anti-aircraft guns, and a troop of tanks. And all were used in effectively the same way despite their different tactical characteristics. They were placed in position to plug a gap and where they could fire at targets of opportunity. In other words, they were left in place, and it was clear that the mortars, when I arrived in May 1993, had been in situ for a considerable period. And they were still there when I left in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "in situ," could you just explain what you mean. Did they move from one spot to another spot in the same vicinity or were they on the same immediate spot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Base plates had not moved. When a mortar is fired, because of the angle of firing, the base plate - that is, the platform on which the barrel sits - is pushed into the ground, and the more rounds that are fired, the further it is pushed into the ground. It was clear that these mortars had been in exactly the same position for a considerable period. This was most unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The crews that operated these mortar batches, from your observation of them, is there anything you can say about their general quality and training?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was -- we tend -- all professionals tend to make a mystery of their own profession. However, there is nothing particularly mysterious about firing mortars and the skills can be learned relatively quickly. And it seemed to me that the people of the troops in question had the requisite skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that for a period of time, you were posted at the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. I was there as liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your function as liaison officer in those barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: My first job was to deputise for the commander of the UNMOs in the Lima area. But following on from that, part of the task was to liaise with the headquarters staff of the Sarajevo Romanija corps of the Bosnian Serb army in order to pass on information to them and receive information from them regarding war activities in the area, and also to negotiate, where required, cease-fires and to monitor cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you pass on any particular type of information to them in respect to the circumstances that civilians were undergoing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, we did. On occasion, we would receive information from our headquarters inside the city that a particular area was being sniped or being shelled. And we would then go to the liaison office which was directly across the hallway from our living and working accommodation, and we would discuss the issue with the liaison officers of the corps, and we would request a cease-fire or request cessation of shelling, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were -- what was the result of these requests that you made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In many cases, directly the liaison officer would ring the brigade in question and would request them to cease firing. On other occasions, they would explain that an attack had been launched against a Bosnian Serb position by the Armija, and that they were merely responding to such aggression. So sometimes the request was successful and sometimes it was not, but there was always an explanation as to why it would not be successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said many times they would contact the brigades and ask them to stop firing. How did you become aware of this? At this time, did you speak --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The liaison office was in two separate rooms directly across the hall, as I said. Both were obviously in -- had telephone systems. Occasionally, the liaison officer would go into the other room and make the request by telephone, but sometimes he would make the call in front of me. He would actually ring the brigade in front of me or request the person on the switchboard to ring the brigade and speak to somebody in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you understand B/C/S? By that time, did you understand the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not a lot, no, but enough to know they were doing what they said they were doing. "Brigada" and "brigade," you know, very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who were the liaison officers that you made these reports to about the sniping and shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The chief of the team was Colonel Zarkovic. Colonel Zarkovic, and his two main assistants were Major Misa Indic, and Captain Brane Luledzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These -- I beg your pardon. Who, at that time, was the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija corps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The corps commander at the time was General Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see him in this Court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever personally make any protest or report to him about the sniping or shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I did not. Not personally to the general. We dealt through the liaison team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe for us the physical circumstances in which the UNMOs lived at Lukavica barracks. You said you had your accommodation across from the liaison office.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. We were on the ground floor of the main corps headquarters building, or what seemed to me to be the main corps headquarters building, just directly inside the gates of the barracks. And when one went in the main door and turned to the left, there was the press and information office, and beyond that was the UNMO accommodation and offices which comprised a working area, a sleeping area, and a small kitchen. We shared the bathrooms of the remainder of the people living in the corps headquarters, and similarly, we could eat with them. Beside us was a conference room, and directly across the hall, as I said, were the liaison offices. Upstairs, then, seemed to be the office of the corps commander and his senior staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see Major General Galic at Lukavica barracks while you were posted there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how often would you see him there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Frequently. Frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Frequently meaning? Could you approximate what you mean by "frequently"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Whenever he would be coming in or out of the building I would see him. Travelling places. On the stairs, in the hallway. Perhaps not daily, but certainly numerous times in a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you observe how, if in any way, he related to his liaison officers to whom you made your reports about the sniping and shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: He spoke to them as a commander would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, what do you mean by "as a commander would"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally, a commander relies upon his staff for particular jobs to be done. He can't, obviously, do them all himself. So he would have persons responsible for security, for personnel matters, for logistics, and in this particular case, because of the nature of the operation, liaison. So I saw him speak to Colonel Zarkovic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you have been in the army for over 30 years.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you made observations of the weapons in Yugoslavia while you were there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you observed them while they were in use?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to hand to the witness Document P3675.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I proceed, may I inquire of the Court: The document, of course, has been translated into B/C/S but since the working languages of the Tribunal are English and French, I don't know if we need to, at a later stage, tender the documents in both languages. I imagine we only need to tender them in one of the working languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the Chamber deems it not necessary that a B/C/S translation is tendered. On the other hand, if there would be any problem with the translation disclosed to the Defence, then, of course, it's up to the Defence to do whatever they think would be necessary in order to object against a document disclosed to them. But for the work of the Chamber, it's not necessary at this very moment. And if, for example, there would be differences between the translation and the original, then of course, it might become necessary. But at this very moment, the Chamber does not insist on having a B/C/S version tendered. And we do understand that a B/C/S version has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This document is a document called "Weaponry in the former Yugoslavia" and effectively it's a bit of a dissertation on artillery in general and in its use in the wars in the former Yugoslavia, complete with pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does it deal with, to some degree, with small arms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It does, yes. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we could say, I think, that it is a brief description of some of the weapons that were used in the former Yugoslavia while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Some of the weapons, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You -- do you agree with everything that you see -- well, may I just put the question this way: Have you seen the document before this day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have seen the document before, and you will note that I have initialled every page of it. And I have handwritten certain comments which I felt would not necessarily disagree completely with what was said but perhaps clarify some of the items in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just have a quick look at these clarifications. You made some clarifications on page 3 of the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by the first one. If I made read it: "Larger mortars may have a less sophisticated system than guns."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Point 4 there: "Mortars do not have a recoil system or a heavy barrel tube to absorb the force of the propellant charge, thus limiting the size of a propelling charge and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it possible to read more slowly, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. It says: "Mortars do not have a recoil system or a heavy barrel tube to absorb the force of the propellant charge, thus limiting the size of the propelling charge and hence its range and pay load." That is not strictly accurate. Larger mortars in particular do have a recoil system, however, it is a less sophisticated system than guns or Howitzers, hence my written comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next comment you made, could you explain it? I'll read it: "True in offence only. Only one third of range in enemy territory in a defensive role."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This refers to the sentence: "Their siting also endeavours to have 60 to 80 per cent of their maximum range reaching into enemy territory." Generally, in conventional teaching, mortars are sited forward in offence. That is, they would be approximately one third of their effective range behind the forward edge of the battle area, the front line, if you will. So that for a mortar with a range, a planning range, of say 6.000 metres, it should be planted about 2.000 metres behind the FEBA in offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is a FEBA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Forward Edge of the Battle Area. However, in a defensive situation, the mortars are deployed much further back, with two thirds of the range, the planning range being between them and the forward edge of the battle area, so that same mortar would be 4.000 metres behind the front line, in defence. Hence my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also commented that, if I may read: "Can be fired from a normal truck, but reinforcement is desirable." Could you just briefly explain what that clarification is about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Light mortars - 60 mortars - medium mortars - 81 and 82 millimetre mortars - can be fired from vehicles. Now, a truck can be used as a firing platform for these weapons, providing sandbagging, for example - bags filled with sand - are placed under the base plate to give a cushioning effect. The recoil is not great, but without some protection, it would damage a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the last comment you made, is that in respect to heavy mortars, "they need to be dismounted from the wheels when they are firing."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The comment made is that heavy mortars are towed by a vehicle or prime mover and dismounted from their bogie wheels for firing. That is not the case. It is not necessary to dismount them. In actual fact, it is counterproductive to dismount them because it prevents quick -- because it prevents quick removal of the weapon from the area after it has fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I take it that, apart from those clarifications, you agree with the contents of the document as a basic description of the weapons that were used in the former Yugoslavia while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Commandant. Now, can you tell the Court briefly, if maybe you could enumerate what are the methods that can used to determine from where a mortar has been fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The detection of a mortar is actually quite easy because it has a very loud signature, that is, it makes a very loud noise when it is fired. Even at low charge - charge 0, charge 1 - it is still a very, very loud weapon. It can be detected by a sound ranging system, accordingly. That is, by a series of microphones placed in a line across a large distance and connected to a central processing unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It can -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just go on. You said notwithstanding that it might be on a low charge, it could be detected. Could you just briefly, if you could, explain what you mean by "low charge" as opposed to a high or medium charge.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay. A mortar projectile is a fixed bomb. However, it requires additional charges to give it further range. So a standard mortar could be fired between, say, charge 0 and charge 6, each number referring to an additional increment of propellant which comes by way of either a satchel or a horseshoe which fits on the base of the round. So that a mortar firing on a low charge would have a short range. As each increment is added for a given angle of elevation, the round goes further, generally, as I say, up to about seven charges. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said one of the ways the place where a mortar is fired from could be detected is by sound. Are there any other ways?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It can also be detected by radar. They are radars in existence since the 1960s which will detect the exact location of a mortar which has fired just one round. Another way, of course, is if the observer can see the mortar firing. And that, obviously, is the most accurate of them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When a mortar impacts at a target, does it normally leave any particular markings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It depends very much on the ground on which the mortar lands. A mortar which lands on concrete or asphalt leaves a very clear signature. A mortar which lands on soft ground or earth leaves a much more indeterminate crater, but there is always a crater of one type or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is there a method -- or I think I could just take you straight there. Have you any experience in crater analysis and could you explain to us what that is about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Crater analysis is the examination of a crater, generally a fresh one, which has been caused by a projectile and which -- from which one may determine the direction from which the projectile has come and, in certain circumstances, the range from which it is fired, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that after your posting in Sarajevo, you were posted in Zagreb. Were you so posted in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was. I was, at that time, acting chief operations officer in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the UNMO organisation in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on or about the 11th of February, 1994, did you receive any particular mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did. Subsequent to the Markale incident of the 5th of February, the chief military observer was directed to put together a team of experts to investigate the Markale bombing. I was appointed by him to form part of that team due to my background as an artillery officer with extensive artillery experience both in Ireland and in the Middle East, and the fact that I was an instructor in gunnery in our own artillery school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have any particular title in that team of experts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: For political reasons, after arriving in Sarajevo, I was designated as the technical advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did the team receive terms of reference or guidance, instructing them as to how they should perform the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you so abide by the terms of reference and perform the investigation as a team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of our ability, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: We arrived, if I remember, on the night of the 10th or early in the morning of the 11th. I think it was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when was the report due to be presented?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It had to be presented, if memory serves me, by the 15th, which was four days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to the scene of the Markale?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: We certainly went to the scene on the morning of the 11th. We also went to the scene on the 12th, interviewed witnesses and other persons with a direct interest in the case, and produced our report by the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you contribute to the preparation of the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did the report include annexures?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I process to tender to the witness a copy of the report that he spoke of. However, I should advise the Court that there are some problems with legibility in some parts of the report. We have done everything I know possible to obtain completely legible copies. The parts which are not legible are -- do not amount to the bulk of the report, and I would submit that the sense of the report can still be ascertained. We have asked for searches to be conducted in Geneva and in New York to see if we could obtain a better copy of the report and we have conducted quite a few searches in the OTP itself since last year to see if there might have been here a better copy of the report. We have not been able to locate a better copy. However, we have located a document which is identical to the summary of the report which is at the front of the report which I would later seek your leave to tender to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps I should give you the opportunity to respond to these observations while Mr. Stamp is tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first -- if it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave the opportunity to Ms. Pilipovic, but I didn't hear from her, so I was about to take it that...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness stated that he had written the report, if I understood him correctly, maybe it would be useful for us to get some clarification from the witness in respect of the illegible portions of the text. So if we can perhaps have the assistance of the witness with these illegible parts of the text, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there are no objections. There's, rather, a suggestion how to clarify the issue, Mr. Stamp. This will certainly be of assistance to you, I take it. And please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document you have in front of you, marked P2261, is that a copy of the report with the annexures?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the back of that document, do you see a document with these numbers on it? I should say the third-to-last page of that document, 0026-4146 and it goes on to 48.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you would look at what is marked Appendix 2 to Annex C of the report, and I -- and that is the part numbered 0026-4146.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that Document numbered 0026-4106 a cover page to the UNPROFOR report in respect Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: From sector HQ Sarajevo, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was a report of one Captain Verdy, who had done an analysis of the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the front page of that report is annexed to the report of the United Nations team of experts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those last three pages, is it correct to say, the last three pages of the document you have in front of you, from 0026-4126 to 41 -- to 0026-4148, would be the UNPROFOR report with the front page plus the other two pages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: What I would say is that it is a very specific report from one individual from sector HQ Sarajevo, with which I disagreed fundamentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would ask, for the sake of convenience, if for the next couple minutes, Mr. President, Your Honours, I could just deal with matters of organising the documents for ease of reference by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We had a short break in between. It is 11.00 now. If you could do it quickly, please proceed. Otherwise, we would have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I wonder, and I'm in the Court's hands, if the explanation of the witness is sufficient or if it will be necessary to separately mark those last three pages. He has explained that these last three pages are -- or they include the report plus the other two pages of the report is annexed in the body of the UNPROFOR team of experts report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber for the moment feels that it's sufficient, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the benefit of the Chamber, may I draw the Chamber's attention to that part of the report numbered 0026-4112 to 0026-4113. Those two pages were written in the French language, which is one of the languages of the Tribunal, however, we have an English translation, which I would designate as P2261.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you might have noticed, all members of the Chamber both read and speak French as well, so for the Chamber it's not necessary. I do understand that the Defence, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is also speaking French. So I think for the time being, I'm just wondering, but I have to give it some more thought on if this case would ever go on appeal, whether perhaps then a translation should be prepared. But you say it's there already, but this Chamber at this moment can do with the French version. I see the French -- the English version is the -- yes. I see it is there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The English version is done or was done because the witness might be asked questions about that part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you request the witness on this part of the report, do the interpreters' booth have the English versions available to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the document numbered -- or the pages marked 0026-4093 to 0026-4095, is that a summary of the report --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- those pages? And from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, could you please repeat the numbers because they do not appear in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Commandant, I'm referring to 0026-4093 to 0026-4095.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to hand to the witness a document marked P2261A. Could you have a quick look at that document, and when you're ready, could you tell us if this document, P2261A, is substantially the same as the first three pages of the report which you said is a summary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is substantially the same. It is, in fact. It was prepared for the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That document, Mr. President, is a document which we located which could assist the Court in respect to the legibility issues in respect to the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look at the page of the report. At the top, it is 6 of 46, and it is Annex A, and the number at the bottom is 0026-4097. Can you say who were the members of the team, having a look at that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite clear that the team leader was Colonel Michel Gauthier, from Canada; team members were Lieutenant Colonel Nikolay Rumyantsev, from Russia; Major Sahaiser Khan, from Pakistan; Captain Jose Grande, from Spain; Captain Lavarde, from France; and technical advisors John Hamill, that is myself; and Sergeant Chef Dubant, from France.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's convenient to you, it's convenient to the Chamber at this moment as well. We will adjourn until a quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I indicated that I would give a decision about the documents used during the examination of the witness of last Friday after the break. If you do not mind, I'd rather do it after we have finished the examination of this witness, and I also then will give a decision on the documents tendered by the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, which had not yet been done. So perhaps now, Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at Document P2261A. Item number 2 on that document, does that describe the scope of the investigation or the terms of reference which confined the scope of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is it correct that the investigation mandated was to complement earlier investigations conducted by the United Nations, and that the investigation should be confined to the crater analysis and the related technical aspects of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you are confined to include all relevant physical information concerning the explosion, technical analysis, and also, if you could, any relevant findings in respect to culpability?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, as so stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your investigation was on the basis of this terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on page 3 of that document, item 17, there is a finding in respect to culpability. The last three lines read: "There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired from either side." Was that your findings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was our findings. That is an accurate assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was based on the investigations that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As confined by the terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it possible, on the basis of those terms of reference -- if I may ask you this question: Was it possible with those terms of reference to make any finding in respect of culpability in the circumstances of the investigation, the physical investigation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: What I would say is that the findings that we produced were the most comprehensive possible, given the limitations of the methods and the events surrounding the incident, that given also the technical nature of the mortar bomb and its use, there was no possibility whatsoever of determining culpability in the case of this particular explosion due to the distance between it and the front lines of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you started the investigation on the 11th of February.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you completed your investigations, or you wrote your report when, can you say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: We finished the report at approximately 3.30 on the morning of the 15th of February, 1994. That is, four days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that investigation included interview of UNMO personnel, discussions with both parties, as well as various analyses of the physical evidence in the market?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. We interviewed persons from sector Sarajevo who had been in the area at the time. We interviewed both UNMO and sector Sarajevo personnel. We spoke also to members of the Armija and also to members -- to a specific member of the Bosnian Serb army during that period who had been designated by their respective authorities to assist us in our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the deadline for you to produce your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the team did a variety of crater analyses.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your findings, that would be on page 3, was that the explosion was caused by a conventional factory-produced 120 millimetre high explosive mortar bomb which detonated upon impact with the ground.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. That was very, very specifically written to exclude the possibility that the mortar detonated on contact with a stall approximately one metre above the ground, which was the initial report given by a so-called crater analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The cause of the explosion in that paragraph is that the bomb appears to have been launched in a conventional manner from a 120-millimetre heavy mortar tube.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. That was stated because one of the parties had reported to the investigating team that they believed that the bomb had been launched by a pneumatic device from a specified address within the city of Sarajevo, not far from the location of the market. The team discounted that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the team's technical and physical examination of the site, was it possible that the traces you saw there could have been caused by a statically-exploded bomb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Definitely not. As stated, the explosion was caused by conventional factory-produced 120 millimetre high explosive mortar bomb. No other explanation possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you personally conduct crater analyses at the scene?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many did you conduct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I conducted two; one on the morning of the 11th and one on the morning of the 12th. We had a change in our team leadership between the two periods, between the morning of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, and the new team leader decided that he wanted it done again so we went and did it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many methods of crater analysis did you use?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Personally, I used two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe the first method of analysis that you used.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have to look at my own notes again, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You made a written report in respect to your crater analysis and findings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did. Oh, yes. A very specific type of mark --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment. May I direct you to Annex 4 to Annex C. That is written in the top right-hand corner, page 18 of 46, or 0026-4109 in the bottom right of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that a copy of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is a copy of my report, 26-4109, yeah. Now, the first method was called a fuse tunnel method. When a mortar bomb hits the ground, the force of it hitting the ground -- the force of its traverse through the air causes it to continue into the ground for a short distance. And because of the makeup of the bomb, there is a piece at the end, the tail, which is nonexplosive. The head is explosive; the tail is not. So the tail continues and follows the direction that the fuse took when it was -- when it hit the ground, it follows the same direction. So the fuse makes a tunnel into the ground, and the tail follows behind. Meanwhile, the body has exploded into every direction. So what I did was I got a stick and I placed it in the fuse tunnel as excavated. Now, this was not as accurate as it might have been because it had been one week since the explosion, or near enough one week since the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you continue with your explanation, we'll get back to that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you did your examinations, when you arrived there first, had the site been secured by the local police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was secured by the local police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you did the fuse tunnel method. Can you continue.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: So what you do is you place the stick into the ground, into the fuse tunnel, and this gives a direction. And by taking a bearing, a bearing with a compass, you determine the direction from which the round had come, from which the bomb had arrived. So in this particular case, the direction given was something in the region of 0300, 0330 to 0360 grid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to explain that briefly. The figure which you just gave us --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It's mils. There are 6.400 mils in a circle. So a direction of around 0360 would mean generally north-northeast. That is, between north and northeast. It would have come in from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just going to go briefly into that. We sometimes measure directions in terms of degrees, and you have mentioned mils. Can you just explain briefly the relationship of mils to degrees.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There is approximately 17.78 mils in one degree, so a mil is an inherently more accurate method of determining exact direction. As I said, there are 6.400 mils in a standard circle. So a quarter circle would be 1600, and 400 would be a quarter of a quarter, as it were. So you're looking at a quarter of a quarter from north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And 6.400 mils would correspond to a complete circle in the same way that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- degrees would correspond to a complete circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, your finding of approximately 300 to 330 to 360 mils, was that in respect to mils from magnetic north, true north, or geographic --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Grid north. Grid north. Geographic north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to the Court the distinction between grid north and magnetic north, and could you explain it having regard to the method you used with your compass.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: All right. Firstly, magnetic north is not fixed. It is a location generally in the north of Canada which varies because the axis of the earth actually varies. So magnetic north is not a fixed point. To compensate for that, geographers place a grid of squares on a map, working from west to east and from south to north, to get northings and eastings. And every location on the earth can be determined by means of the grid. So grid north is preferable to use than magnetic north, which is not stable. So what I did with my compass, because magnetic north is all that a compass can measure or can point to, and there is a variation, one must determine the variation. And the way I determined the variation with that specific compass - because again, all compasses are different - was I took two known points, I stood in one, I measured the grid bearing to the other. In this particular case, if memory serves me, I used a junction at the airport and the hill of Ilinaca, which is a prominent feature to the east of the airport, determined the grid bearing, measured the bearing with my compass, and found that there was a variation between the two, naturally. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is, a variation between the grid bearing and magnetic north.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, in this case of about 60 mils. There was about a 60 mil difference. So what I had to do whenever I measured any other bearing with my compass was to add 60 mils to get the true grid bearing in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said approximately 60 mils.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 60 mills.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it then that in February 1994, magnetic north was approximately 60 mils away from grid north.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And your findings are in terms of the figures you gave us in mils, is it in respect to magnetic north or grid north? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Grid north. Always, always grid north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Other members of the team did examinations and made findings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were their findings in respect to grid north or magnetic north?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Also grid north. All professionals would use grid north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you used another method of crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. I used a method of two poles aligned on the centre of the splash pattern. There are a number of ways of so doing. A splash pattern is very, very distinctive, and one can, for example, align two poles on the wings of the splash pattern, and the -- angled between them, the centre of the angle between them is the direction away from which the round -- the direction towards which the round came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, this splash pattern is caused by what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The splash pattern is caused by splinters when the round explodes on the ground. What happens is the round explodes into numerous small pieces of hot metal which gouge out a pattern on the concrete or asphalt, or indeed on earth or mud, and in the case of concrete or asphalt, especially concrete, they are quite distinctive and they form two long wings, in the case of a mortar, away from the location of the explosion, back towards where the round came from, but at an angle, at a wide angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you make any finding as to whether or not the mortar round was fired in a normal manner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was my opinion from the physical evidence that was produced to us that it was fired in a normal manner in that we were given the tail of a mortar, the markings of which corresponded to markings which had been noted by the first UN team on the scene on the 5th of February and which had been taken down by them when the round was still in the crater. So the same number was stamped on the fuse -- sorry, not on the fuse but on the propellant charge that there was on the mortar. The primary cartridge, which looks like a shotgun cartridge, was struck on the bottom by a firing pin, thus indicating that the round had been launched from a normal mortar and not by other means. It wouldn't be safe to be playing around with a round which had the primary cartridge struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that there was a technical analysis. Could you have a look at the second page. That is a page marked 346, 0026-4094.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry, can you give me that number again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And a detailed and technical analysis based on the physical evidence in the market and surrounding area was conducted. And further, I'd like you to have a look at the page marked 846 in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On that page, under the heading "Physical Evidence," at item F, there is a reference to fragments found in the crater and in the surrounding area. If I may read from the beginning: "The team's technical analysis was conducted based on the following evidence: The crater found in the marketplace, the tail-fin assembly of a mortar bomb extracted from the crater, the markings on the ground surrounding the crater, the damage to the stalls --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last item, item D I mentioned, was, "...the damage to the stalls surrounding the crater, the dimensions of the marketplace including the buildings surrounding it, and fragments found in the crater and in the surrounding area." Were fragments found in the crater and in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: They were fragments found in the area but they were very, very small pieces and of no benefit to the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
