utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that every shootrep and every intrep was reported. The information was very comprehensive, and the location where the round fell, were known, was mentioned. So yes, we certainly had specific information on specific locations on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a matter for the records, I am wondering if the answer is the information was very comprehensive and the location where the round fell "where known" was mentioned or is it "were known"? I think I heard the witness say "where known."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I think, for the record, the transcript should read "where known," and not "were known."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if this reflects your answer better, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have the transcript on my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, because I have the word "were," and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be where known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Hamill, read your answer on page 87, line 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes, in the sense that every shootrep and every increp --" i-n-c-r-e-p -- "was reported. The information was very comprehensive and the location where the round fell, where known, was mentioned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where known, that's w-h-e-r-e.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's because in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not always the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- previous line there's also the word "where." It's two times where, with w-h-e-r-e. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not always the case that the location where the round fell was known because it was heard but not seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, as you were giving us your answer, you mentioned the hill of Mojmilo. Will you agree with me that during your tour of duty, the hill of Mojmilo was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It certainly was, and indeed they sniped from there into Lukavica and sometimes at military observers, too. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And you are telling us, therefore, that the troops of the BH army were controlling the Mojmilo hill and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- and that they opened sniping fire from there, aiming at Lukavica. In that part of the city, was there any fighting between the troops of the army of BH holding the positions on Mojmilo and the army of Republika Srpska whose positions were, we've just said Donja Kotorac and Lukavica? Can you tell us if in that part of the city there was any fighting between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was a very quiet part of the city. There was very little by way of combat activity. As I mentioned, there was sniping from Mojmilo towards Lukavica, towards the Serb-held part of Dobrinja, for example. But it was generally quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Hamill, you are speaking about the sniping activities from both the positions of the troops of the army of BH. Can you tell us, how frequent were such sniping activities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sniping in that area was infrequent. Sniping in the area of Grbavica was quite frequent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in the area of Grbavica, there was very frequent fire, did you, during your stay, get any information as to from which parts of the city was the sniping fire opened against Grbavica? Did you establish which were the facilities, the structures, from which sniping fire was aimed at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It seemed to me that the fire was coming from the area around -- generally around the Hotel Bristol, that general area. From Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say from Hrasno, do you have any information if Hrasno was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska or the BH? And can you specify the positions with regard to Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Hrasno was the front line, more or less, between the Armija and the VRS. And on one side of the stadium -- in general terms, on one side of the stadium you had the VRS; on the other side, you had army of BiH. And the sniping was coming into Grbavica from the Armija side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the army, you mean the BH army, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Army of BH, yes. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, during your tour of duty and activity at your post, did you have any information as to the type of armament of the BH army? Did you receive the information from your team members observing the part of the city controlled by the BH? What kind of weapons did they use?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: They were quite lightly armed, generally. They had mortars. We were aware they had mortars. We knew they had some tanks. They had some artillery guns but very, very few. Generally, it was rifles, machine-guns, standard infantry-type weapons, RPGs, that is, rocket-propelled grenades.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the area of Sarajevo, were you ever present at the fighting which took place in some parts of the city between the troops of the army of BH and the army of Republika Srpska? Or more specifically, did you eyewitness one of -- some attack of the BH army? Can you confirm for us that the troops of the army of BH also conducted some actions in which it participated as an attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. I was present in Vogosca in early July during one particular attack when the Armija, Armija BiH, attacked VRS lines and were responded to by first small arms and then fairly heavy artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about BH army attacks on the road to Pale? Do you have any information if there was any fighting in that part of the city between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There was certainly one major attack at the end of May in which the army of BiH attacked uphill towards Zlatiste. It was an infantry attack without any proprietary fires, and it was repulsed by the BSA with very small losses on their part. But my understanding from my colleagues on the Papa side was that there were very large Armija BiH casualties, well in excess of 100. It was directly after that that we monitored that particular area, driving up and down the road, looking at positions, inspecting positions, seeing what could be seen and just generally implementing the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, since you communicated both with the representatives of the army of Republika Srpska and the BH army, can you tell us what did the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska wear, that is, whether they had any uniforms and what kind of, and the same question goes to the members -- regarding the members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was policy amongst the military observers that we did not mix with combat personnel of the side which we were not monitoring. So I had no contact with members of the Armija BiH at that time. I only had contact with members of the VRS. They were generally armed -- they were generally clothed in a type of camouflage combat uniform, dark brown. Some of them who appeared to be more militia than Armija, as it were, more gendarmerie/militia type, wore a kind of blue-grey camouflage uniform. But generally, the soldiers wore a greeny-olive camouflage uniform. Not everybody had the full uniform. Some more some civilian clothing with bits of uniform because, of course, it wasn't a regular army in that sense. It was an army of people who perhaps by day were farmers and by night were soldiers, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hamill, you are confirming that in the part of the city controlled by the army of Republika Srpska, that members of the army of Republika Srpska were in residence of the parts of the city which was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. That is, that the residents of this part of the city were also members of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Practically every person that I met on the VRS was a native either of the outskirts of Sarajevo or had lived perhaps in Hrasnica, perhaps in Centar, perhaps in Bascarsija, and had come out to the outside around April, May, June of 1992. So most of them, but not all, most of them were Sarajevans. There were others. There were people from Crnokar [phoen], for example, there were people from Herzegovina. But generally, the people -- certainly 95-plus per cent of personnel there were locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, thank you for your answer. Today during your examination-in-chief, explained that you heard protests, that you received various protests from your associates who were controlling and observing the part of the city in the hands of the BH army. Can you tell us, what was the form of these protests that you received and that you, as you told us, forwarded and informed Mr. Indic about? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: If Major Indic was there, we would speak to him. If he wasn't, it would be Captain Lucia [phoen] or perhaps one of the other staff who were present. There were a number of others. We would receive information that shelling was going on in a particular area, perhaps an area monitored by Papa 5 or Papa 3 or whoever. And we would go to the office and say, there is shelling going on in this area. What's happening? It must be stopped. And at that stage, they would not -- they would often know already that IT was happening, naturally, because they were the corps headquarters. Or if they didn't know, it was because they had, perhaps you might say it was an independent activity going on. But generally, they were aware of what was going on and had a prepared answer, if you will, if they didn't wish to stop the shelling or shooting. Or sometimes, they did anyway, they stopped it or they caused it to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, can you tell us the following: Would the shelling in the part of the city controlled by the BH army, after you had received such a protest, can you tell us if it is -- what kind of information did you receive? What unit was involved, and what was targeted, or to make myself clear, can you tell us precisely during that period of time from which area and when and from whom did you receive information as to the part of the city under shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: We received that information specifically from UNMO teams working in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you receive information from other teams working in the area, can you be more precise? Can you tell us, this information, if it was oral information, did you also receive such information in writing? And did such written information include the exact name of the formation and the part of the city shelling and whether there were any combat activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: When we received the information, it was by radio, because obviously doing it by letter or by hand would take too long. It took -- it could take two hours to reach Lukavica from the centre even if it were possible to go through, which it wasn't always. So there was no sense in sending written information that a shelling was going on. Our job was to cause the shelling to stop. That had to happen instantly. There was no point in having it go on for two, three hours before going into the liaison office and saying "stop it". So the question isn't really relevant. It came by radio from the teams. Now, obviously they wouldn't say to us, "It's the 105th Brigade headquarters that's being shelled." They would say "There is shelling going on in Papa 4's area. It's in this particular grid square." It was not up to us to question the Papa teams on their information in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to when the Papa team would inform that shelling was underway? Specifically you mentioned the case of the 105th, and I suppose you mean the 105th Brigade of the BH army. Now, when you get such a report that a certain part of the city is under shelling, would you know -- if teams of UNMOs would go to the site straight away, would they draw up a record of it? Would they inform you about it as a member of Lima on the other side, and was such information or was such record then forwarded on in the form of protests?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: What happened was as soon as a shelling occurred, incoming or outgoing, it was reported by the appropriate team. If it was outgoing from their area, it went out as a Shootrep, a shooting report. If it was incoming into their side, in other words, if their area was being shelled, it was reported immediately in the form of an incident report, an INCREP I-N-C-R-E-P. So that this was an instant response, and we were made aware instantly of what was happening because we could hear it going over on our radio set. We had the radio set on 24 hours a day. From 7.00 in the morning until 11.00 at night, we had our own channel specifically for the UNMOs. We heard everything that was happening with every team. The reports were comprehensive insofar as it was possible to make them. One paragraph was kept for the written form. It wasn't kept or it wasn't sent over the radio. And that was the type of target. But it was a written report at the end of the day, and every day's reports were filed and kept. So it's quite possible to go back and look at any specific day and see what was being shelled at that time. Generally, when we went into protest, it was because a normal civilian area with no apparent military value was being attacked. This was the information that we were given by our people on the Papa side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would this be a suitable moment for you to interrupt your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, our Court schedule tells us that at 4.00 we stop, in the afternoon. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, not 9.30, 9.00. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Hamill out of the courtroom so that we can deal with one or two technicalities. Would you please follow the usher, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we still have to deal with two issues. First of all, I still owe you the decision on the medical records we discussed this morning. These are the -- it's the medical records especially of -- I don't want to make any mistakes. It's about the medical records of Ramiza Kundo. Mr. Stamp, the Chamber has decided that the evidence as it is presented now cannot be admitted. On the other hand, that it would be admissible if there would be a -- if it would be the best legible copy with a translation without any unclarity and if a proper explanation is given why elements of the document which are not well visible in the text itself. And you might remember that we discussed, for example, the first name of a doctor where we only see his initial. If you could -- if the Prosecution could give us a proper explanation of what has happened during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the various translations made of these documents, especially in this respect where we find translation elements which are not there in the original copy of the document -- I wouldn't say the original document, but the original copy of the document. And finally, I inform the parties that the Chamber thinks that on the basis of the objections made until now, and given the authentication of the document as given by the witness itself, there's no need on this basis for any additional authentication for this moment. And as I told you, it's on the basis of the objections made until now. Of course, if there's anything else, we'll hear about it. That's the decision on the medical records of the Witness Kundo. Then we still had to decide, Ms. Pilipovic, on two documents the Defence tendered. One is an official note. That is the Exhibit D75, which is an official note drawn up by Mr. Jusufbegovic. The second one is a handwritten statement of Hilmo Kundo. Since I've heard no objections, not on Friday, not today, they are both admitted into evidence. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
